Themes

urlet ships six visual themes inside the single binary, and an administrator can upload additional stylesheet-only themes at runtime. A compiled-in theme is code: an Askama template directory under templates/themes/<key>/ plus one embedded CSS file. An uploaded theme is a CSS file stored on the persistent volume; it reuses the base page layout because Askama templates are compiled into the binary and cannot be added at runtime.

KeyNameNotes
verdantVerdant SystemsThe v1.2 production design; also the base templates and fallback. Ships both palettes and the persisted light/dark control
auroraAurora GlassDark glass command centre with a fixed sidebar. Dark-only: no light palette, so the light/dark control is hidden
paperPaper LedgerEditorial paper ledger. Ships both palettes and the light/dark control
signalSignalBrutalist signal board. Ships both palettes and the light/dark control
gildedGilded CircuitArt Deco ivory/emerald/gold. Ships both palettes and the light/dark control
swissSwiss TelemetrySwiss grid with numbered sections. Ships both palettes and the light/dark control
custom-…UploadedA stylesheet added from Admin → Themes; reuses the Verdant templates

The five non-default compiled-in themes are the designs proposed in the closed pull requests #5, #6, #7, #9 and #10. They were ported to the v1.2 page model rather than frozen at their original feature set.

Every design except Aurora follows prefers-color-scheme until the visitor picks a mode, and then honours that choice in both directions: its stylesheet carries the dark palette twice, once behind @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) guarded by :not([data-theme="light"]) and once behind :root[data-theme="dark"]. A new port that skips the second copy still follows the operating system, but its light/dark control would be a lie — the test every_dual_palette_design_serves_the_system_and_the_explicit_palette catches that.

The browser chrome is the one surface CSS cannot reach: a theme-color meta tag is selected by a media query, and a media query cannot see data-theme. A design that paints the chrome (Signal) therefore marks its two tags with data-theme-mode="light"/"dark"; the media queries stay the no-JavaScript path, and theme.js switches the matching tag on once the mode is resolved.

How a visitor's theme is chosen

  1. urlet_theme cookie, when it names an enabled theme (compiled in or uploaded).
  2. Otherwise the administrator's default.
  3. A cookie for a disabled or unknown theme is ignored and the default is used.

The picker is a native <details> element and works without JavaScript. When switching is open to everyone, a visitor who is not signed in sees it too, so a look chosen on the landing page survives the sign-in that follows. The cookie is HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, lives for one year, and is Secure when the instance is configured for secure cookies. It is a cosmetic preference, not a per-user database column; a new browser starts at the default. The picker's Site default entry clears the cookie and follows the administrator's default again.

Like the language picker, the switch endpoint is a GET. It only writes a cosmetic cookie; it never changes data or permissions. A cross-site top-level navigation can therefore change the look, but cannot grant access or alter an account.

Templates and the fallback

templates/ at the repository root is both the Verdant theme and the fallback. It also owns the shared chrome: the footer in templates/base.html carries the two user-visible links every design keeps — the attribution link to the upstream repository (partials/repo_link.html, labelled GitHub) and the API reference at /docs (partials/api_docs_link.html, labelled API). A compiled-in theme directory may override any page:

Pages with a large amount of v1.2-only state (quotas, domains, groups, invites, settings) are shared through Askama macros in templates/content/. A theme overrides the chrome and the public/auth pages from its original design, and wraps the shared body in its own shell. This keeps every theme feature-complete when the product grows, at the cost of the older designs looking more like the base content on dense admin pages. The shared src/assets/theme-ui.css fills in classes those older stylesheets did not know about; it uses :where() so the original design always wins where it has an opinion.

The template is selected at compile time by themed_page! in src/routes/pages/themed.rs. Each page context gets .themed(), and the macro generates one small wrapper per theme that dereferences to the same context. Askama's compile-time field checking therefore still applies to every theme. Uploaded themes select the Verdant wrapper at compile time and only replace the stylesheet URL; they join the catalogue through the administrator workflow below.

Administrator workflow

  1. Open Admin → Themes (/app/admin/themes).
  2. Upload a custom stylesheet: give it a name, an optional description, then drag a .css file onto the drop zone (or click it to choose a file). Choose an appearance — Follow system, Light only (white) or Dark only (black). The upload appears in the catalogue immediately, enabled.
  3. Tick the designs that should be offered. At least one theme must stay enabled.
  4. Pick the Default theme. It must be enabled; visitors without a cookie see it.
  5. Choose Who can change their theme:
    • Everyone — members and visitors may switch (the default). A visitor without a session gets the same picker on the pages that carry site chrome: the landing page, sign-in and registration, and error pages.
    • Administrators only — administrators keep the picker for previews; members do not see it, and a direct switch returns 403. A visitor without a session is sent to the sign-in screen instead.
  6. Preview applies a theme to the current administrator only, then returns to the theme page.
  7. Save. The selection is applied immediately; no restart is needed.

An uploaded theme can be renamed, have its appearance and stylesheet replaced from its edit page. Delete removes the catalogue row and the CSS file; a theme that is currently the default cannot be deleted, so choose another default first. The original file name is kept for display only; the stored path is derived from a generated key and the content hash.

The policy is enforced when pages render, not only by hiding the picker. Under Administrators only, non-admin accounts and anonymous visitors always render the site default; an existing urlet_theme cookie (including one set while the policy was Everyone) is ignored. Administrators keep the picker and can use Preview to inspect any theme, including one that is not enabled yet, without changing the visitor-facing default. The preview cookie lasts one hour. A normal picker click or Stop preview leaves preview mode.

The redirect surface — a short link, its password prompt and the splash pages — never offers the picker, even under Everyone. Those pages stay minimal and only follow a cookie the visitor already has; the picker is one click away on the landing page they point back to.

The same selection is available as GET/PUT /api/v1/admin/themes. The JSON API accepts enabled, default and switching; omitted fields keep their value. Uploads themselves are a browser multipart form: the JSON API is read/update for the catalogue, not a file-upload endpoint. GET includes uploaded themes with "custom": true and a hashed css_url.

Custom theme storage

ItemLocation
Metadatacustom_themes table in the SQLite database
Catalogue stateA matching themes row (key, enabled, default, order)
Stylesheet<URLET_THEMES_DIR>/<key>-<content hash>.css
Default directory<URLET_DATA_DIR>/themes
DockerThe urlet-themes volume, mounted at /data/themes

The content hash is part of /assets/custom-themes/{key}?v=<hash>, so replacing a stylesheet changes the URL and cannot be masked by the one-hour asset cache. The metadata and the file live on the persistent /data volume; a restart rebuilds the in-memory registry from the database and the upload remains selectable.

The upload is deliberately restricted:

  • a CSS file: the upload field expects one; accept=".css,text/css" and the drop zone's filename check are browser-side conveniences, and the server never looks at the extension. Validation runs on the content: UTF-8, 256 KiB at most, no control characters, and at least one { and one };
  • at most 32 custom themes per instance;
  • absolute external references and cross-origin url(...) are rejected: http://, https://, ftp://, data:text/html and data:image/svg are refused anywhere in the file, and a url(...) may not point at another origin. CSS escapes and comments are decoded first, so u\72l( cannot smuggle one past. The scan matches text rather than parsing CSS, so a protocol-relative reference inside another functional notation — image-set("//host/a.png"), for example — is not caught; the CSP is the second line of defence;
  • no @import, expression(...) or legacy behavior;
  • served as text/css with X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so it cannot turn into an HTML document.

An upload also chooses how the palette behaves:

  • Follow system keeps the ordinary light/dark control and follows the operating system until the visitor picks a mode.
  • Light only and Dark only force data-theme="light"/"dark" on the server, hide the light/dark control, and cannot be overridden by a saved browser preference. This is the "pure white" / "pure black" choice.

Uploaded CSS is served after the Verdant stylesheet, so a small colour or layout override composes with the default design and wins the cascade. The base stylesheet is linked from the upload panel for reference. Custom uploads never change the document templates: they can restyle every page, but cannot add markup or scripts.

Adding a compiled-in theme

  1. Add a variant to ThemeKey in src/services/theme.rs (key, name key, description key, CSS URL, palette policy). A design that ships only one palette declares it through is_dark_only/is_light_only; appearance() is the single source of truth for the catalogue's appearance field and its light-only/dark-only badges.
  2. Add the CSS under src/assets/themes/<key>.css and register it in src/assets.rs and the /assets/themes/{key} route.
  3. Add the catalogue strings to the three src/i18n/*.json files.
  4. Create templates/themes/<key>/ with at least base.html, app_base.html, landing.html, the auth/link/splash/error pages, the admin tabs and the app pages. Reuse the content macros for the dense app pages. Load theme.js in base.html's <head>, and render the picker and the light/dark switch exactly once per page: in the top bar of landing.html and app_base.html, and through partials/site_tools.html (switch, picker plus language switcher) wherever the design keeps its footer tools. A design that empties footer_lang for its own top bar must put the tools there instead, as Swiss's auth pages do. Copy the data-theme/data-theme-lock attributes of templates/base.html onto <html>, so a forced palette is marked on the document as well as in the catalogue.
  5. Add templates/themes/<key>/... paths to every themed_page! call. Keep the Verdant entry in each invocation: it is also the fallback used when a page has not listed a newly added theme yet.
  6. With the key, templates and CSS registered, add the theme to ALL and the admin tests, then let db::themes::ensure_defaults insert the catalogue row at startup. Leave the migration seed untouched: released migrations are checksum-protected, and startup seeding covers new and existing databases.
  7. Run cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test and scripts/smoke.sh.

Deliberate limits

  • Uploads are stylesheets, not templates. The CSP stays default-src 'self' and the binary stays self-contained; a custom theme cannot add markup or scripts.
  • Uploads are administrator-only. There is no per-user theme marketplace or per-account upload quota; the site-wide catalogue stays the single source of truth.
  • No remote theme fetch: the server never downloads a stylesheet, and external url(...) / @import are rejected in addition to being blocked by the CSP.
  • No fine-grained per-account permission: the policy is site-wide (all or admin). The existing user-group feature toggles cover per-group data capabilities, not cosmetics.
  • Every design except Aurora ships both palettes and the same persisted light/dark control; the control is a cosmetic preference, so it never needs a per-account column. Aurora is dark-only by design and has no light palette to offer, so it hides the control instead of shipping a dead one.
